results.name: new-york
results.question: A split state
results.popup:
New York in 1828: 36 electors

In the pie: Andrew Jackson, 20 votes; John Quincy Adams, 16 votes.

Who chose the electors: Voters, by districts; the district electors then chose two more (McPherson v. Blacker, 1892).

White men: No property or tax rule since an 1826 amendment; the 1821 constitution had already eased the rules for white men.

Free Black men: The 1821 constitution set a new rule for Black men only: own property worth $250, pay tax on it, and have been a citizen for three years. In 1825 only 298 Black men in the whole state qualified.

Source for the rules: Constitution of 1821, Art. II, sec. 1, and the 1826 amendment; Peter J. Galie, Albany Law Review (the 298 figure)

Today's state outlines, with West Virginia shown as part of Virginia, as it was in 1828. Territories are not shown. Women could not vote in any state in 1828.

results.name: virginia
results.question: Explain why: Virginia
results.popup:
Virginia in 1828: 24 electors

In the pie: Andrew Jackson, 24 votes; John Quincy Adams, 0 votes.

Who chose the electors: Voters, statewide.

White men: Had to own 25 acres with a house, 50 acres of unimproved land, or a town lot with a house (law of 1785). A new constitution in 1830 loosened the rule.

Free Black men: The 1785 law excluded "free negroes or mulattoes".

Source for the rules: Act of 1785 (Hening, Statutes at Large, vol. 12)

Today's state outlines, with West Virginia shown as part of Virginia, as it was in 1828. Territories are not shown. Women could not vote in any state in 1828.

results.name: south-carolina
results.question: Question the source: no popular vote
results.popup:
South Carolina in 1828: 11 electors

In the pie: Andrew Jackson, 11 votes; John Quincy Adams, 0 votes.

Who chose the electors: The state legislature, as it did until 1860; voters had no direct say in choosing the president's electors.

White men: No property was needed: owning 50 acres or a town lot, or living in the district six months, was enough (1810 amendment). This rule was for state elections.

Free Black men: The constitution allowed only free white men (Constitution of 1790).

Source for the rules: American Presidency Project; South Carolina Encyclopedia

results.name: tennessee
results.question: Free Black men who could vote
results.popup:
Tennessee in 1828: 11 electors

In the pie: Andrew Jackson, 11 votes; John Quincy Adams, 0 votes.

Who chose the electors: Voters, by districts.

White men: No property was needed: owning land in the county, or living there six months, was enough (Constitution of 1796).

Free Black men: Could vote until 1834, when a new constitution shut them out.

Source for the rules: Constitution of 1796, Art. III, sec. 1

results.question: Explain why: the legislature chose
results.popup:
Delaware in 1828: 3 electors

In the pie: Andrew Jackson, 0 votes; John Quincy Adams, 3 votes.

Who chose the electors: The state legislature; voters had no direct say in choosing the president's electors.

White men: Had to have paid a state or county tax. This rule was for state elections.

Free Black men: Allowed only white men (Constitution of 1792, as quoted in a Delaware archives document).

Source for the rules: American Presidency Project (1828 election); Delaware Public Archives

results.name: georgia
results.question: Explain why: first popular vote
results.popup:
Georgia in 1828: 9 electors

In the pie: Andrew Jackson, 9 votes; John Quincy Adams, 0 votes.

Who chose the electors: Voters, statewide, for the first time (the legislature chose in 1824).

White men: Had to have paid all taxes due (Constitution of 1798).

Free Black men: Free Black men were not treated as citizens, so they could not vote; the clause itself doesn't say white.

Source for the rules: Constitution of 1798, Art. IV, sec. 1; Cooper v. Savannah (1848)
